Empirical Research Plan: Long-Term Earnings Effects of Job Displacement in Pennsylvania, 1977-1986
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
   • Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) implemented as an event-study in calendar time and “event time” (years relative to displacement).  
   • Justification  
     – Plant closures/mass-layoffs are plausibly exogenous to any one worker’s productivity or effort.  
     – We observe individuals for multiple years pre- and post-displacement, so we can difference out permanent worker heterogeneity with individual fixed effects and common macro shocks with calendar-year fixed effects.  
     – The event-study formulation lets us (i) test the parallel-trends assumption, (ii) trace the entire earnings trajectory, and (iii) allow for heterogeneous dynamic effects.

2. Treatment and Control  
   • Treatment variable  
     – Treated = 1 for a worker starting in the first calendar year in which he/she is coded as displaced because the prior employer experienced a plant closure or a mass lay-off (>30% reduction in employment, following BLS definition).  
   • Control group (counterfactual)  
     – Workers in the same industry × county × pre-event calendar year who (a) keep their jobs, (b) are employed continuously at firms that do not subsequently shut down, and (c) match on pre-event earnings decile, age, and tenure (propensity-score or exact-cell matching).  
     – Rationale: they face the same local labor-demand shocks except for the idiosyncratic closure, satisfying the “common shocks” requirement.  
   • Treatment timing / event date  
     – Event year = 0 is the calendar year of displacement.  
     – Leads: k = –5,…,–1; Lags: k = 0,…,+10 (we can follow longer if data permit).  
   • No running variable → RDD not used.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
   A1. Parallel Trends: Absent displacement, treated and control workers would have continued on parallel earnings paths.  
       ‑ Plausibility: We can test visually and statistically using the pre-event leads. Matching on pre-period earnings and tenure strengthens plausibility.  
   A2. No Anticipation: Workers do not substantially change labor-supply behavior before the displacement is announced.  
       ‑ Plausibility: Most plant closures are announced with short notice; we will drop observations if the closure was announced >1 year ahead.  
   A3. SUTVA / No Spillovers: Control workers are not indirectly affected by the same closure (e.g., through local labor-market slack).  
       ‑ Plausibility: Some spillovers likely exist. We mitigate by selecting controls in industries not directly linked to the displaced plant and by controlling for county×year shocks.  
   A4. Stable Composition: Attrition (migration out of state, death) is not systematically different across groups or can be observed and controlled for.  
       ‑ Plausibility: We observe earnings from unemployment insurance records only while individuals remain in PA coverage. We will track out-migration flags and re-weight or bound results.  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
   1. Differential Pre-Trends  
      – Test: Plot event-study coefficients for k<0.  
      – Remedy: Exclude plants with gradual downsizing, add individual linear pre-trends, or use synthetic-control re-weighting within DID.  
   2. Local Labor-Market Shocks (spillovers)  
      – Include county×year fixed effects; alternatively, choose controls in neighboring counties unaffected by the shock.  
      – Cluster standard errors at the plant (or county) level.  
   3. Selective Attrition / Missing Earnings for Movers  
      – Show results on: (i) all workers assigning zero earnings to non-observed, (ii) inverse-probability weights for staying in-state, (iii) bounding (Lee bounds).  

5. R Code Outline (TWFE Event-Study with fixest)  

```r
# --------------------- 0. Packages ---------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)   # fast fe estimators
library(modelsummary) # nice tables
# --------------------- 1. Load Data --------------------
pa <- read_csv("pa_displacement_77_86.csv")

# --------------------- 2. Construct Variables ----------

# 2.1 Identify event year (first displacement)
pa <- pa %>%
  arrange(worker_id, year) %>%
  group_by(worker_id) %>%
  mutate(displaced = if_else(event_type %in% c("closure","masslayoff"), 1L, 0L),
         ever_disp  = max(displaced),
         disp_year  = if_else(displaced == 1, year, NA_integer_)) %>%
  fill(disp_year, .direction = "downup") %>%  # first event year
  mutate(event_time = year - disp_year) %>%
  ungroup()

# 2.2 Keep workers w/ at least 3 yrs pre data
pa <- pa %>% group_by(worker_id) %>%
  filter(min(event_time, na.rm=TRUE) <= -3 | ever_disp==0) %>% ungroup()

# 2.3 Create matched control sample (very simple P-score example)
pre_vars <- pa %>% filter(year == (disp_year - 1) | ever_disp==0) %>%
  select(worker_id, ever_disp, pre_earn = earnings, age, tenure, industry, county)

# Estimate propensity to be displaced
ps <- glm(ever_disp ~ log(pre_earn+1) + age + tenure + factor(industry)+factor(county),
          data = pre_vars, family = binomial)$fitted.values
match_cut <- quantile(ps[pre_vars$ever_disp==1], probs = c(.01,.99))
keep_ids <- pre_vars$worker_id[ps > match_cut[1] & ps < match_cut[2]]
pa <- pa %>% filter(worker_id %in% keep_ids)

# 2.4 Event-study dummies
max_lag <- 10; max_lead <- 5
for(k in -max_lead:max_lag){
  pa[[paste0("E",k)]] <- as.integer(pa$event_time==k)
}
# omit E-1 as reference

# --------------------- 3. Main Regression --------------
es_formula <- as.formula(
  paste0("log(earnings+1) ~ ",
          paste0("E", c(-max_lead:-2,0:max_lag), collapse=" + "),
          " | worker_id + year"))
est <- feols(es_formula, data = pa, cluster = ~plant_id)

# --------------------- 4. Robustness: add county×year FE
est2 <- feols(update(es_formula, . ~ . | worker_id + year + county^year),
              data = pa, cluster = ~plant_id)

# --------------------- 5. Output -----------------------
etable(est, est2, drop = "worker_id|year|county", se = "cluster")
```

6. Expected Results  
   • Direction: Negative and persistent earnings effects.  
   • Magnitude (bench-marking to U.S. JTPA and displaced-worker studies):  
     – Year 0/1: –25% to –30% of pre-displacement annual earnings.  
     – Year 5: –15%.  
     – Year 10: –10%, with large heterogeneity (older, long-tenure workers suffer more).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
   C1: Pre-trend balance visually/statistically verified  …… 1  
   C2: No anticipation (exclude early announcements) …… 0.8 ≈ 1  
   C3: Correctly specified treatment timing  …………………… 1  
   C4: No spillovers / SUTVA  ……………………………………… 0 (questionable)  
   C5: Stable sample composition / attrition handled …… 0.5  

   Overall score ≈ 3.3 / 5 → generally credible but needs careful robustness work, especially on spillovers and attrition.
